clue.text: Benny Hill?

parts.note: The surface hands you the comedian; the setter is thinking of BEN, which is what Scotland puts in front of its highest lumps — Nevis, Lomond.
So the question the clue is really asking is what you call a hill grand enough to be a Ben, with the question mark owning the upgrade.

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here — no fodder, no letters to move. Benny Hill was the comedian; Ben Nevis is the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ben is Scotland's word for a high peak, so a hill big enough to be a Benny has been promoted clean out of the hill class.

clue.text: Hero knocked over nuclear fuel

indicators.note: Something knocked over ends up lying the other way about, so the letters are read from the far end back.

parts.note: N is the standard shortening of nuclear, as in N-bomb
oil is the fuel — and N + OIL, knocked over, is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuclear fuel' reads as one thing on the surface and is two abbreviations stacked underneath, which is the whole trick of a four-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Hero → LION: a lion is the standard image of courage, and English calls a brave man a lion of the fight or lion-hearted.

clue.text: 11 stopping Spanish team getting close again

indicators.note: A stopping is what a dentist pushes into a gap to plug it, so one lot of letters goes inside the other.

parts.note: Real Madrid, Real Betis, Real Sociedad — Spain's leagues are full of Reals
11 across is EL SALVADOR, and the country goes about on ES plates

explanation.walkthrough: A cross-reference number stands for another entry in this grid, so 11 has to be solved before this one gives up its two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: close again → RESEAL: the RE- prefix does the 'again', and sealing an envelope or a jar is one particular way of closing it.

clue.text: Suppose Big Bird's turning up to support Trump?

indicators.note: In a down entry, letters that turn up are read from the foot of the column towards the top, which is backwards.
To support a thing is to sit underneath and hold it, so this piece goes below the other in the column.

parts.note: Trump is a president, PRES for short — the question mark admits it is one example
the big bird is an EMU, climbing the column

explanation.walkthrough: Big Bird and Trump are both real people-shaped things on the surface, and neither is wanted: the clue needs a flightless bird and an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Suppose → PRESUME: both are verbs for taking something as true without proof, PRESUME leaning on the confidence of the assumption.

clue.text: Mother starts to upset Lily Savage

parts.note: MA is the short form of mother

indicators.note: The start of a word is its opening letter, so only the front of each word that follows is taken.

parts.note: the opening letters of Upset Lily

explanation.walkthrough: Lily Savage was Paul O'Grady's drag act, which is what the capital letter is for; the clue wants 'savage' as a plain verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Savage → MAUL: as a verb, to savage someone is to attack and tear at them, which is exactly what an animal does when it mauls.

clue.text: Award sounded crazy for playwright

parts.note: the Academy Award is an Oscar

indicators.note: The word asks for the noise a word makes rather than its spelling, so you write down what your ear hears.

parts.note: crazy is WILD, and WILD said aloud is how the surname is heard

explanation.walkthrough: Wilde wrote The Importance of Being Earnest, which 13 down is quietly sitting next to. The silent E is the entire homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: playwright → OSCAR WILDE: the author of Lady Windermere's Fan and An Ideal Husband, so the trade names one of its most quoted practitioners.

clue.text: Bad-tempered types last to get up for walk

indicators.note: The letter at the foot of the column climbs to the top while every other letter keeps its place.

parts.note: trolls are the bad-tempered types, under bridges and under the line

explanation.walkthrough: This is a rotation, not a reversal: only one letter travels and the rest hold their order. Turned round properly it would read SLLORT.
explanation.definitionFit: walk → STROLL: a stroll is a walk taken slowly and for pleasure, the unhurried end of the same idea.

clue.text: Flexible practitioner to support animated character

parts.note: the flexible practitioner is a yogi, the one who does the yoga
to bear a weight is to support it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises a bendy expert holding something up; the answer is the picnic-basket thief of Jellystone Park.
explanation.definitionFit: animated character → YOGI BEAR: the Hanna-Barbera cartoon bear, so the general phrase is pointing at one particular drawn star.

clue.text: Strength from dog shaking off lead

indicators.note: A dog that shakes a thing off is rid of it, so the letter named next is dropped from the word.

parts.note: the basset hound is the dog
a dog's lead here is its leading letter, the B at the front, which goes

explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is about walking a dog, and 'lead' is the one that changes job: leash on top, first letter underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Strength → ASSET: an asset is something you have going for you, so this is strength in the sense of a plus point rather than muscle.

clue.text: Year in Spanish Main's ending soon

parts.note: año is Spanish for year

indicators.note: The ending of a word is its final letter, so all but the last of Main is left out.

parts.note: the last letter of Main

explanation.walkthrough: The Spanish Main was the Caribbean coast of the empire, which is why the two halves of the wordplay read as one place name.
explanation.definitionFit: soon → ANON: anon is the old adverb for 'in a little while', still alive in 'see you anon' and all over Shakespeare.

clue.text: Disney princess left queen over trouble in country

indicators.note: One thing lying over another covers it, so the queen's two letters wrap round what follows.

parts.note: Elsa, the ice queen of Frozen
L is the standard abbreviation for left
Victoria Regina, VR, the crossword's queen
much ado about nothing — ado is trouble, and it goes inside VR

explanation.walkthrough: VR for Victoria Regina is worth banking — setters reach for royal cyphers constantly — and a Disney princess keeps the surface in the snow rather than in Central America.
explanation.definitionFit: country → EL SALVADOR: the smallest republic in Central America, so the plain word is defining it by example.

clue.text: Book that is set in strange land

indicators.note: To set a stone in a ring is to embed it, so two letters are planted inside the rest.
Strange means not as it should be, and letters that are not as they should be have been shuffled.

parts.note: the four letters of LAND, rearranged
i.e. is the Latin shortening of 'that is'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' in a cryptic is very often one of the Bible's, and this is the prophet who spent a night in with the lions.
explanation.definitionFit: Book → DANIEL: one of the books of the Old Testament, named for its prophet, so the general word names it by example.

clue.text: Value of New Romantic EP

indicators.note: Something made new has been remade from what was there, so the letters following are rebuilt in another order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: New Romantic bands and their EPs make a tidy 1981 surface, and the capital R is pure disguise — it is just the fodder's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Value → IMPORTANCE: both are nouns for how much something matters, value in the sense of weight or worth rather than price.

clue.text: Football team crush defensive formation

parts.note: to mill grain is to crush it
the wall of players lined up in front of a free kick

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are football words too, which is what makes the join invisible — and the club's nickname is the Lions.
explanation.definitionFit: Football team → MILLWALL: the club from Bermondsey in south London, so the general phrase is naming one side by example.

clue.text: Shot regularly dismissed Ollie Pope

indicators.note: Shot means wrecked — nerves, a gearbox — and wrecked letters will not stay in the order they were handed to you.
Send away the letters that fall at regular intervals and only the ones in between survive.

parts.note: drop the second and fourth letters of OLLIE and OLE is what is left

explanation.walkthrough: Ollie Pope bats for England, so the surface is a morning at the Oval. The answer is a papal name, and a lion besides.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope → LEO: fourteen popes have reigned under the name, so the office is defining one of its commonest regnal names by example.

clue.text: North Korea's leader hacking into computer's digital printing devices

indicators.note: To hack into a machine is to get inside it, so one set of letters is planted within another.

parts.note: the computer is an iPad, and the setter's ’s hands over the S
N is the compass abbreviation for north
the leader of KOREA is its first letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' is the pivot: not electronic here but of the fingers, which is why a state hacking story ends up at a fingerprint.
explanation.definitionFit: digital printing devices → INKPADS: digital is doing its older job, of the fingers — an ink pad is what a fingertip presses into to leave a print.

clue.text: Study of depression cut short

indicators.note: A thing cut short loses its far end, so the final letter comes off.

parts.note: a dent is a depression in a surface, and it loses its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' is the room, not the act of learning — and a den is also where the animal running through this grid lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Study → DEN: a den is the small private room at home you shut yourself in to work, which is what an English house calls a study.

clue.text: Most generous and good of Poirot to make a comeback in case

indicators.note: Anything making a comeback arrives the other way round, so those letters are read from the far end.

parts.note: Poirot is Belgian, so his word for good is BON, arriving backwards
lest means in case, as in 'lest we forget'

explanation.walkthrough: 'In case' looks like joinery holding the sentence together and is really four of the seven letters, which is where the clue hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Most generous → NOBLEST: noble describes generosity of spirit rather than of pocket, so the noblest gesture is the most big-hearted one.

clue.text: Swindling trick from man in uniform

indicators.note: The little word does the placing: the man is put within the other word rather than beside it.

parts.note: uniform means all alike, the same throughout
the king is a man on the chessboard

explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' is the adjective, not the soldier's outfit the surface promises, and that swap is the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Swindling trick → SKIN GAME: to skin someone is to fleece them, so a skin game is a rigged game run to strip the mark of his money.

clue.text: Denis Villeneuve's right to film movie in US city

indicators.note: To film a surface over is to lay a coat across it, so one piece is wrapped right round the other.

parts.note: Villeneuve is a Québécois director, and droit is French for right
Spielberg's E.T., the shortest movie in the crossword's stock

explanation.walkthrough: A director shooting a film is the surface, and both halves of the wordplay keep it: his French 'right' and a two-letter picture.
explanation.definitionFit: US city → DETROIT: Michigan's motor city on the Canadian border, so the general phrase is naming one place by example.

clue.text: Carriage clock's face cutting clumsy cleaner

indicators.note: The clock's letter cuts in among the others instead of standing outside them, so it joins the letters being rearranged.
A clumsy worker knocks things out of position, and letters knocked out of position have to be put back in some new order.

parts.note: the face of the clock is the front of the word, its C
anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a domestic scene with a clock and a hopeless cleaner; the answer is Victorian transport named after a royal duke.
explanation.definitionFit: Carriage → CLARENCE: a clarence is a closed four-wheeled horse carriage named for the duke who became William IV, a word kept alive by crosswords.

clue.text: Chemist replacing parts of large Whopper

indicators.note: Re-placing is putting the pieces down somewhere else, so the two halves swap ends.

parts.note: large is big
a whopper is an outrageous lie; the burger is there for the surface

explanation.walkthrough: Justus von Liebig is worth banking: his name is on the condenser in every school laboratory and on the meat extract that became Oxo.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemist → LIEBIG: the German who founded organic chemistry teaching, so the trade is naming one of its famous practitioners.

clue.text: Personal assistant admits one form of word blindness

indicators.note: To admit a guest is to let them in, so the assistant takes the next letter inside itself.

parts.note: Amazon's Alexa is the personal assistant on the shelf
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.walkthrough: A voice assistant that reads things out for you is a neat surface for a condition about not being able to read.
explanation.definitionFit: form of word blindness → ALEXIA: alexia is the medical name for losing the ability to read while the eyes themselves still work.

clue.text: 2 followed by Tesla obliquely

indicators.note: What follows comes after, so the second piece is written on the end of the first.

parts.note: the answer to 2 down is a lion, and Narnia's is Aslan
T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density

explanation.walkthrough: Tesla the car firm is the misdirection; the unit named after Nikola Tesla is what the wordplay wants, and it is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: obliquely → ASLANT: both are adverbs meaning at an angle, so a picture hung aslant is hanging obliquely rather than square.

clue.text: Distressed maid in pantry retreating from flying insect

indicators.note: Distressed furniture has been knocked about on purpose, and letters knocked about will not stay in their given order.
The little word does the placing: the shuffled letters sit within the other word rather than beside it.

parts.note: the pantry is the larder, which retreats to REDRAL

indicators.note: An army retreating goes back the way it came, so the pantry is read from its last letter to its first.

parts.note: the letters of MAID, distressed, and dropped inside REDRAL

explanation.walkthrough: A distressed maid in a pantry is a whole Victorian novel in five words, and not one of them is about a butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: flying insect → RED ADMIRAL: the butterfly with the orange-red bands across black wings, so the broad description covers it by example.

clue.text: Artist trimmed long hair

indicators.note: A trim takes a bit off the end, so the artist loses his final letter.

parts.note: Manet, the French painter of Olympia, with the end trimmed off

explanation.walkthrough: Manet and Monet are both four-fifths of something else, which is why the crossword reaches for them so often.
explanation.definitionFit: long hair → MANE: a mane is the heavy hair along a horse's or a lion's neck, and the word is used of anyone with a big head of it.

clue.text: Heartless bum in prison

indicators.note: Without a heart is without a middle, so the centre letter of the word is taken out.

parts.note: to bum a cigarette is to cadge one; the heart of it, D, goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' is the verb here, not the noun the surface is pointing at: to bum a fiver is to cadge one.
explanation.definitionFit: prison → CAGE: a cage is a barred enclosure, and prison slang has used it for a cell as long as there have been bars.

clue.text: Musical Youth finally escaping from Jaws

definitions.note: The S belongs to a title rather than to a plural: the show is called Cats but it is one musical, so the singular definition is right.

indicators.note: The word points at the end of what precedes it, so only its closing letter is in play.

parts.note: to jaw is to talk away, so 'jaws' is CHATS

indicators.note: What escapes leaves the place it was being held in, so that letter comes out of the longer word.

parts.note: the closing letter of YOUTH, which escapes

explanation.walkthrough: Musical Youth had the hit and Jaws had the shark, so the surface is all pop culture and neither half means what it seems to.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical → CATS: Lloyd Webber set T. S. Eliot's cat poems to music and ran for twenty-one years, so the general word names one show by example.

clue.text: Hotel California charges old person

indicators.note: To charge a glass or a gun is to load it, so the hotel is loaded with what comes before.

parts.note: the hotel is an inn
CA is the postal abbreviation for California

explanation.walkthrough: The Eagles' song holds the surface up, and the answer is an inn with a state loaded into it. CA for California is worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: old person → INCAN: an Incan belonged to the Andean empire Pizarro destroyed, so 'old' is doing the work of ancient here.

clue.text: I mention getting hammered before you can say Jack Robinson

definitions.text: before you can say Jack Robinson

indicators.note: Hammered means drunk, and a drunk cannot be relied on to keep anything in the order it was given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole idiom at the end, which is why it reads as surface; 'I mention' does nothing for the sentence and everything for the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: before you can say Jack Robinson → IN NO TIME: both are idioms for 'immediately', the long one being the Georgian ancestor of the short one.
